Content: I don't know if I am the only one?? So basically Nintendo launches their current console, changes a few features and calls it a new console. I think Marques's review is great, he touched on all of the technical stuff and what we need to know. But from a consumer standpoint I don't see the logic in buying this if you already have a switch, specifically an OLED switch as I believe this can be hooked up to your TV. Nintendo's strategy team is really smart,. they read the market, specifically the American market and found an emotional gap they can fill for now as some consumers were thirsty for something new and different. To think of the Nintendo Switch 2 as a new console is just crazy!!!!

Content: $500 and you don’t even own the Switch 2, just a license to use it. If Nintendo decides you’ve violated their terms (which could be for anything), they could revoke access to the switch or even demand it be sent back to them. I’ve read that if power levels go outside their limits, even from a repair job, it might brick the system and every time it gets bricked you have to pay around $20 to Nintendo to get it unbricked no matter the reason. It’s all about squeezing as much money from us as possible. Nintendo is the only ones that can repair it so you gotta pay them to fix it, pay more for console itself, more for all the games, and in the end, you don’t even truly own any of what you just bought. Content: I used to work on giant telecom  switches and routers and one of the biggest feedback we had for the physical engineering team is that they put the pins on the backplane.  Pins bend sometimes if you do something bad, or something gets stuck somewhere.  Pins should be on the removal part. Otherwise you end up having to replace the most expensive and hardest to replace part.  Nintendo should have engineered the pins onto the controller, and have them slide in and out when it is put into the dock, since they allow its use as a mouse.  Controller easier and cheaper to replace if something gets broke.

Author: @sn0ren
Content:
I think this new mouse feature could be much bigger than people realise. There is a substantial number of gamers who still play strategy games on their PC primarily because of them being much easier to control with a mouse. But these kinds of games could easily be run on a console if the controls weren't in the way. 

Xbox and PS5 supports connecting a mouse, but unfortunately barely any games take advantage of this, probably because not many users bother with buying and connecting one. Switch 2 having this feature included out of the box will make it more sensible for developers to support this. Lots of FPS games would benefit hugely from having mouse support.

Author: @jonathan130
Content:
I genuinely think the Switch 2 could fail, or at least underperform compared to its predecessor. And the reason comes down to one key thing: competition.

The Switch 2 is expected to be Nintendo’s main console for the next 7+ years. That means developers will be locked into working with relatively weak hardware all the way until around 2032. Meanwhile, the competition in the handheld gaming space is heating up fast. New devices with cutting-edge performance are being released frequently, and when it comes to raw specs, the Switch 2 will become outdated almost immediately. Sure, if you're buying it solely for Nintendo exclusives like Mario or Zelda, that’s fine. But gaming is so much more than just first-party titles, and when other handhelds start offering broader game libraries (games like GTA6) and better performance, the Switch will look less and less appealing to the average consumer. Sure, the Switch 2 might hold up for now and maybe even for the next three years. But as time goes on, it will become increasingly problematic for Nintendo.

Now let’s talk about cloud gaming, because whether people like it or not, that is the future. Not today, but very likely within the next 10 years. Devices like the PlayStation Portal already let you stream PS5 games in beautiful quality for half of the Switch’s expected price. And when the PS6 drops? Nintendo users are going to feel the gap hard. Yes, internet connectivity is still a limitation today. But once 6G arrives and global internet infrastructure improves, and it will, game streaming will become seamless, even in rural areas or while traveling. Xbox is already working on a portable cloud gaming device, and other players are entering the market too.  The competition is exploding. Plus, you don’t even need a separate device for cloud gaming, you can access it right from your phone, TV, computer, or almost anything else. It’s that accessible. Back when the original Switch launched, Nintendo basically had no serious rivals in the handheld space. But things have changed. The handheld market is expanding rapidly, and expectations are rising with it. So if I'm being honest and realistic, the Switch 2 might be setting itself up to fail, not because it will be a bad console, but because the rest of the world is moving forward faster than Nintendo seems willing to.

What is all this competition really leading to, and what does the future of gaming consoles look like? In the coming years, traditional consoles will likely become obsolete. The cycle of releasing new hardware every 7 years will fade away. Instead, gaming will move toward cloud-based streaming, where you simply subscribe and play, no need for powerful hardware at home.

And honestly, that's a good thing. It’s far better for the environment. We’ll no longer need to manufacture tons of plastic consoles and physical game discs, then ship them globally. Gaming will become fully digital, more accessible, and more sustainable.

This isn’t just speculation, it’s already happening. The shift is gradual, but inevitable.

Not even while gaming, but browsing the eShop. That's a concern, and maybe an issue that'll get patched. The other issue is that the system keeps asking me to sign in to my account for every single online thing I open, even after selecting 'don't ask me again', so it seems like signing in to the eShop, for example, won't persist when you go into the Nintendo Switch Online app, which is bizarre and irritating. Otherwise, screen looks great and the joy-cons feel really good. I'll see how my impressions of it evolve over time, but the system crashes while browsing the eShop definitely spoiled my excitement for it.
